The estimated annual change rises from approximately \(-0.014\) in 2005 to \(0.127\) in 2010, \(0.268\) in 2015, and \(0.437\) by 2021. This shows that the divergence did not simply increase at a constant rate—the pace of separation became progressively faster over time.

Within the preferred quadratic AR(2) model, the results therefore identify the mid-2000s as the approximate turning point from modest convergence to sustained and accelerating multivariate divergence.



### Does the Multivariate Structure Remain After Removing Time Trends?

The original PCA was based on the observed indicator levels, so part of its structure may reflect the strong long-term trends in the data. To determine whether the same multivariate pattern remains beyond those trends, I repeated the PCA using the detrended residuals for all three indicators.

```{r}
# Standardize the detrended residuals
detrended_pca_data <- three_indicator_detrended %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    daly_residual_z =
      as.numeric(scale(daly_residual)),
    
    mental_health_residual_z =
      as.numeric(scale(mental_health_residual)),
    
    suicide_residual_z =
      as.numeric(scale(suicide_residual))
  )

# Fit PCA to the detrended standardized residuals
detrended_pca_model <- prcomp(
  detrended_pca_data %>%
    dplyr::select(
      daly_residual_z,
      mental_health_residual_z,
      suicide_residual_z
    ),
  center = FALSE,
  scale. = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
# Calculate variance explained by the detrended PCA
detrended_pca_variance <- tibble(
  Component = c("PC1", "PC2", "PC3"),
  Eigenvalue =
    detrended_pca_model$sdev^2,
  `Variance Explained (%)` =
    100 * (
      detrended_pca_model$sdev^2 /
        sum(detrended_pca_model$sdev^2)
    ),
  `Cumulative Variance (%)` =
    100 * cumsum(
      detrended_pca_model$sdev^2 /
        sum(detrended_pca_model$sdev^2)
    )
)

knitr::kable(
  detrended_pca_variance,
  digits = 2,
  caption = "Variance Explained by PCA After Removing Time Trends"
)
```

```{r}
# Extract loadings from the detrended PCA
detrended_pca_loadings <-
  as.data.frame(detrended_pca_model$rotation) %>%
  tibble::rownames_to_column("Indicator") %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    Indicator = dplyr::recode(
      Indicator,
      daly_residual_z =
        "Drug-Use DALY Rate",
      mental_health_residual_z =
        "Mental-Health Death Rate",
      suicide_residual_z =
        "Suicide Rate"
    )
  )

knitr::kable(
  detrended_pca_loadings,
  digits = 3,
  col.names = c(
    "Indicator",
    "PC1",
    "PC2",
    "PC3"
  ),
  caption = "PCA Loadings After Removing Time Trends"
)
```



### Interpretation

After removing the long-term time trends, the first two principal components still explain 98.97% of the remaining multivariate variation. This shows that the three indicators continue to have a strong low-dimensional structure even beyond their shared movement over time.

PC1 explains 76.22% of the detrended variation. Drug-use DALY rate (0.630) and mental-health death rate (0.636) load strongly in the same direction, while suicide rate loads in the opposite direction (-0.445). PC1 therefore represents a contrast between drug-use/mental-health burden and suicide-rate variation after the common time trends have been removed.

PC2 explains a further 22.75% and is dominated by suicide rate (0.895). This indicates that suicide contributes an additional dimension of variation that is not captured by the close relationship between drug-use DALY rate and mental-health death rate.

Compared with the original PCA, the detrended PCA gives a more nuanced interpretation: the apparent overall-burden dimension was partly influenced by shared time trends, while the underlying relationship between drug-use DALY and mental-health death rate remains very strong. PC3 explains only 1.03% and adds little additional information.




### Does the Two-Component PCA Preserve the Multivariate Country Difference?

Because PCA reduces the three standardized indicators to two main components, I checked whether the two-dimensional PCA representation preserves the Canada–U.S. separation observed in the full three-variable space.

```{r}
# Add PCA scores to the standardized dataset
pca_score_data <- standardized_data %>%
  dplyr::bind_cols(
    as.data.frame(pca_model$x) %>%
      dplyr::select(PC1, PC2, PC3)
  )

# Create Canada PCA scores
canada_pca_scores <- pca_score_data %>%
  dplyr::filter(entity == "Canada") %>%
  dplyr::select(
    year,
    PC1,
    PC2
  )

# Create United States PCA scores
us_pca_scores <- pca_score_data %>%
  dplyr::filter(entity == "United States") %>%
  dplyr::select(
    year,
    PC1,
    PC2
  )

# Match countries by year and calculate PCA-space distance
pca_distance <- canada_pca_scores %>%
  dplyr::inner_join(
    us_pca_scores,
    by = "year",
    suffix = c("_canada", "_us")
  ) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    pc12_distance = sqrt(
      (PC1_us - PC1_canada)^2 +
      (PC2_us - PC2_canada)^2
    )
  )

# Compare full three-indicator distance with PC1-PC2 distance
distance_preservation <- multivariate_distance %>%
  dplyr::select(
    year,
    full_distance = distance
  ) %>%
  dplyr::left_join(
    pca_distance %>%
      dplyr::select(
        year,
        pc12_distance
      ),
    by = "year"
  ) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    percent_preserved =
      100 * pc12_distance / full_distance
  )

# Show selected years
distance_preservation_table <- distance_preservation %>%
  dplyr::filter(
    year %in% c(2000, 2005, 2010, 2015, 2020, 2021)
  )

knitr::kable(
  distance_preservation_table,
  digits = 2,
  col.names = c(
    "Year",
    "Full 3-Indicator Distance",
    "PC1-PC2 Distance",
    "Distance Preserved (%)"
  ),
  caption = "Multivariate Distance Preserved by the First Two Principal Components"
)
```

```{r}
# Calculate overall agreement between the two distance measures
distance_agreement <- tibble(
  Measure = c(
    "Correlation",
    "Mean distance preserved (%)"
  ),
  Value = c(
    cor(
      distance_preservation$full_distance,
      distance_preservation$pc12_distance
    ),
    mean(
      distance_preservation$percent_preserved
    )
  )
)

knitr::kable(
  distance_agreement,
  digits = 3,
  col.names = c(
    "Measure",
    "Value"
  ),
  caption = "Agreement Between Full and Two-Component Multivariate Distances"
)
```



### Interpretation

The first two principal components preserve almost all of the Canada–U.S. multivariate separation observed in the original three-indicator space.

Across the selected years, the PC1–PC2 distance retains more than 99.5% of the full three-indicator distance. On average, 99.81% of the distance is preserved, and the correlation between the full and two-component distance measures is essentially perfect (\(r = 1.000\)).

This confirms that reducing the three indicators to PC1 and PC2 results in almost no loss of information about the separation between the two countries. The two-dimensional PCA representation can therefore be used confidently to visualize the main multivariate structure, while PC3 adds negligible information.



### Which Years Show the Greatest Multivariate Separation Between Canada and the United States?

The multivariate distance changed considerably over time. To identify the years with the strongest overall separation, I ranked all country-year distances from largest to smallest.

```{r}
# Rank years by multivariate distance
largest_distances <- multivariate_distance %>%
  dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(distance)) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    Rank = dplyr::row_number()
  ) %>%
  dplyr::select(
    Rank,
    year,
    distance
  )

# Display the five years with the largest separation
top_distance_years <- largest_distances %>%
  dplyr::slice_head(n = 5)

knitr::kable(
  top_distance_years,
  digits = 2,
  col.names = c(
    "Rank",
    "Year",
    "Multivariate Distance"
  ),
  caption = "Years With the Greatest Canada–U.S. Multivariate Separation"
)
```


### Interpretation

The years with the greatest multivariate separation are concentrated in the later part of the study period. The largest distance occurred in 2021 (5.71), followed by 2020 (3.64), 2017 (3.19), 2016 (3.14), and 2019 (2.82).

Four of the five most separated years occurred between 2016 and 2021, reinforcing the earlier evidence that the Canada–U.S. multivariate difference became substantially larger in the later years.

The exceptionally large distance in 2021 stands out, but the presence of several other late-period years among the highest-ranked observations shows that the growing separation is not attributable to 2021 alone.




### Which Years Show the Greatest Multivariate Separation Between Canada and the United States?

I ranked all study years by their multivariate distance to identify when the overall health profiles of Canada and the United States were most different.

```{r}
# Rank years by multivariate distance
largest_distances <- multivariate_distance %>%
  dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(distance)) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    Rank = dplyr::row_number()
  )

# Plot years ranked by multivariate separation
ggplot(
  largest_distances,
  aes(
    x = reorder(as.factor(year), distance),
    y = distance,
    fill = distance
  )
) +
  geom_col(
    width = 0.78
  ) +
  geom_text(
    aes(
      label = sprintf("%.2f", distance)
    ),
    hjust = -0.15,

  ) +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_fill_gradient(
    low = "#56B4E9",
    high = "#D55E00"
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    expand = expansion(
      mult = c(0, 0.10)
    )
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Ranking of Canada–U.S. Multivariate Separation by Year",
    subtitle = "Larger distances indicate greater separation across the three health indicators",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Euclidean Distance",
    fill = "Distance"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "right",
```

### Interpretation

The ranking shows that the greatest multivariate separation between Canada and the United States occurred in the later years of the study period.

The largest distance occurred in 2021 (5.71), followed by 2020 (3.64), 2017 (3.19), and 2016 (3.14). In contrast, most of the smallest distances occurred during the 2000s.

This concentration of the highest-ranked distances in the later years supports the broader finding that the two countries became increasingly different across the combined health indicators over time. The exceptionally large 2021 value stands out, but the strong separation in several earlier late-period years shows that the pattern is not driven by 2021 alone.






### Does the Result Change With a Different Standardization Method?

The main analysis used z-scores to put the three indicators on the same scale. Since unusual values can affect the mean and standard deviation, I repeated the calculation using the median and MAD.

I want to check whether the same Canada–U.S. pattern still appears.

```{r}
# Standardize the indicators using the median and MAD
robust_data <- combined_data %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    daly_robust =
      (daly_rate - median(daly_rate)) / mad(daly_rate),

    mental_health_robust =
      (mental_health_death_rate -
         median(mental_health_death_rate)) /
      mad(mental_health_death_rate),

    suicide_robust =
      (suicide_rate - median(suicide_rate)) /
      mad(suicide_rate)
  )

# Separate Canada
canada_robust <- robust_data %>%
  dplyr::filter(entity == "Canada") %>%
  dplyr::select(
    year,
    daly_robust,
    mental_health_robust,
    suicide_robust
  )

# Separate the United States
us_robust <- robust_data %>%
  dplyr::filter(entity == "United States") %>%
  dplyr::select(
    year,
    daly_robust,
    mental_health_robust,
    suicide_robust
  )

# Calculate the robust distance for each year
robust_distance <- canada_robust %>%
  dplyr::inner_join(
    us_robust,
    by = "year",
    suffix = c("_canada", "_us")
  ) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    robust_distance = sqrt(
      (daly_robust_us - daly_robust_canada)^2 +
      (mental_health_robust_us -
         mental_health_robust_canada)^2 +
      (suicide_robust_us - suicide_robust_canada)^2
    )
  )

# Compare with the original z-score distance
standardization_comparison <- multivariate_distance %>%
  dplyr::select(
    year,
    z_score_distance = distance
  ) %>%
  dplyr::left_join(
    robust_distance %>%
      dplyr::select(
        year,
        robust_distance
      ),
    by = "year"
  )

# Show selected years
standardization_comparison %>%
  dplyr::filter(
    year %in% c(2000, 2005, 2010, 2015, 2020, 2021)
  ) %>%
  knitr::kable(
    digits = 2,
    col.names = c(
      "Year",
      "Z-Score Distance",
      "Median-MAD Distance"
    ),
    caption = "Comparison of Multivariate Distance Using Two Standardization Methods"
  )
```

```{r}
# Check how closely the two distance series agree
standardization_agreement <- tibble(
  Measure = c(
    "Pearson correlation",
    "Spearman correlation"
  ),
  Value = c(
    cor(
      standardization_comparison$z_score_distance,
      standardization_comparison$robust_distance
    ),
    cor(
      standardization_comparison$z_score_distance,
      standardization_comparison$robust_distance,
      method = "spearman"
    )
  )
)

knitr::kable(
  standardization_agreement,
  digits = 3,
  col.names = c("Measure", "Value"),
  caption = "Agreement Between the Two Distance Series"
)
```




### Interpretation

The result stays almost the same when the indicators are standardized using the median and MAD instead of z-scores.

The robust distances are somewhat larger, but the two distance series are almost perfectly related (\(r = 1.000\)). The Spearman correlation is also very high (\(r_s = 0.977\)), showing that the ranking of years changes very little.

Most importantly, both methods show the same pattern: the Canada–U.S. separation is relatively small in the earlier years and becomes much larger toward the end of the study period, with the largest separation in 2021.

This means that the main result does not depend on the choice of standardization method.



### Does AR(2) Still Fit Better After Correcting for the Small Sample?

The time series contains only 22 years. Since ordinary AIC can favor more complicated models in small samples, I also compared the AR(1) and AR(2) models using AICc.

```{r}
# Number of yearly observations
n_time <- nrow(distance_time_data)

# Compare AR(1) and AR(2) using AICc
aicc_comparison <- tibble(
  Model = c(
    "Quadratic + AR(1)",
    "Quadratic + AR(2)"
  ),
  AIC = c(
    AIC(distance_ar1_model),
    AIC(distance_ar2_model)
  ),
  Parameters = c(
    length(distance_ar1_model$coef) + 1,
    length(distance_ar2_model$coef) + 1
  )
) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    AICc = AIC +
      (2 * Parameters * (Parameters + 1)) /
      (n_time - Parameters - 1),
    
    Delta_AICc = AICc - min(AICc)
  )

# Display the small-sample model comparison
knitr::kable(
  aicc_comparison,
  digits = 2,
  col.names = c(
    "Model",
    "AIC",
    "Parameters",
    "AICc",
    "Delta AICc"
  ),
  caption = "Small-Sample Comparison of the AR(1) and AR(2) Models"
)
```



### Interpretation

After correcting AIC for the small sample, the AR(2) model still has the better fit. Its AICc is 35.19 compared with 37.49 for the AR(1) model.

The difference in AICc is 2.31, which gives some support to the AR(2) model, although the advantage is not overwhelming.

Together with the earlier residual checks, this supports keeping the quadratic AR(2) model as the preferred model for the multivariate-distance trend.




### Does the Quadratic Trend Really Improve the Preferred AR(2) Model?

The preferred model uses AR(2) errors, but I also want to check whether the curved time trend is actually needed. I therefore compared a linear AR(2) model with the quadratic AR(2) model using the same error structure.

```{r}
# Fit a linear trend with AR(2) errors
distance_linear_ar2 <- stats::arima(
  distance_time_data$distance,
  order = c(2, 0, 0),
  xreg = cbind(
    year_since_2000 =
      distance_time_data$year_since_2000
  ),
  include.mean = TRUE,
  method = "ML"
)

# Calculate small-sample AICc for both models
n_time <- nrow(distance_time_data)

linear_k <- length(distance_linear_ar2$coef) + 1
quadratic_k <- length(distance_ar2_model$coef) + 1

trend_model_comparison <- tibble(
  Model = c(
    "Linear + AR(2)",
    "Quadratic + AR(2)"
  ),
  AIC = c(
    AIC(distance_linear_ar2),
    AIC(distance_ar2_model)
  ),
  AICc = c(
    AIC(distance_linear_ar2) +
      (2 * linear_k * (linear_k + 1)) /
      (n_time - linear_k - 1),

    AIC(distance_ar2_model) +
      (2 * quadratic_k * (quadratic_k + 1)) /
      (n_time - quadratic_k - 1)
  )
) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    Delta_AICc = AICc - min(AICc)
  )

knitr::kable(
  trend_model_comparison,
  digits = 2,
  col.names = c(
    "Model",
    "AIC",
    "AICc",
    "Delta AICc"
  ),
  caption = "Comparison of Linear and Quadratic AR(2) Models"
)
```
### Interpretation

The quadratic AR(2) model fits the multivariate-distance trend much better than the linear AR(2) model.

Its AICc is 35.19, compared with 49.55 for the linear model. The difference in AICc is 14.36, which provides strong support for keeping the quadratic time term.

This confirms that the Canada–U.S. multivariate separation did not change at a constant rate. The curved trend is needed to describe the faster increase in separation during the later years.


```{r}
# Likelihood-ratio test for the quadratic term
loglik_linear <- as.numeric(logLik(distance_linear_ar2))
loglik_quadratic <- as.numeric(logLik(distance_ar2_model))

lr_statistic <- 2 * (
  loglik_quadratic - loglik_linear
)

lr_p_value <- pchisq(
  lr_statistic,
  df = 1,
  lower.tail = FALSE
)

quadratic_test <- tibble(
  Statistic = lr_statistic,
  `Degrees of Freedom` = 1,
  `p-value` = lr_p_value
)

knitr::kable(
  quadratic_test,
  digits = 4,
  caption = "Likelihood-Ratio Test for Adding the Quadratic Time Term"
)
```
### Interpretation

The likelihood-ratio test is significant (\(\chi^2 = 18.21\), \(df = 1\), \(p < 0.001\)). This shows that adding the quadratic time term improves the AR(2) model compared with using a straight-line trend.

Together with the AICc comparison, this gives strong evidence that the Canada–U.S. multivariate separation follows a curved pattern and increases more quickly in the later years.



### How Certain Is the Estimated Turning Year?

The preferred quadratic AR(2) model places the turning point around 2005.5. I also want to measure the uncertainty around that estimate rather than reporting a single year only.

I used the estimated coefficients and their covariance matrix to simulate plausible values of the linear and quadratic terms and then recalculated the turning year for each simulation.

```{r}
# Select the two time-trend coefficients
trend_coef <- distance_ar2_model$coef[
  c("year_since_2000", "year_squared")
]

# Select their covariance matrix
trend_vcov <- distance_ar2_model$var.coef[
  c("year_since_2000", "year_squared"),
  c("year_since_2000", "year_squared")
]

# Simulate plausible coefficient values
set.seed(3690)

turning_simulations <- MASS::mvrnorm(
  n = 10000,
  mu = trend_coef,
  Sigma = trend_vcov
)

# Calculate the turning year for each simulation
turning_year_sim <- 2000 +
  (
    -turning_simulations[, "year_since_2000"] /
      (2 * turning_simulations[, "year_squared"])
  )

# Keep simulations with positive curvature
turning_year_sim <- turning_year_sim[
  turning_simulations[, "year_squared"] > 0
]

# Summarize the uncertainty
turning_year_ci <- tibble(
  Estimate = turning_year,
  Lower_95 = quantile(turning_year_sim, 0.025),
  Upper_95 = quantile(turning_year_sim, 0.975)
)

knitr::kable(
  turning_year_ci,
  digits = 2,
  col.names = c(
    "Estimated Turning Year",
    "Lower 95% Limit",
    "Upper 95% Limit"
  ),
  caption = "Uncertainty Around the Estimated Turning Year"
)
```

### Interpretation

The estimated turning point is 2005.5, with a 95% interval from about 2003.7 to 2006.7.

This means the shift from a small early decline in Canada–U.S. multivariate distance to an increasing trend most likely occurred in the mid-2000s. The interval is fairly narrow, so the location of the turning point is reasonably stable rather than being tied to one exact year.




## Conclusion and Answer to the Research Question

Canada and the United States showed different mental-health and substance-use patterns over 2000–2021. The United States generally had higher levels across the three health indicators, but the size and composition of the difference changed over time.

PCA showed that most of the multivariate variation could be summarized by two components. The first mainly reflected the shared pattern in drug-use DALY rate and mental-health death rate, while the second was driven more strongly by suicide rate.

The multivariate distance between the countries was relatively small in the earlier years and increased more rapidly after the mid-2000s. This curved increase remained statistically significant after accounting for serial dependence with the quadratic AR(2) model (\(p < 0.001\)).

The main result also remained stable when 2021 was excluded, when suicide rate was removed, when a different standardization method was used, and when the PCA was repeated without 2021.

Overall, the evidence shows that the two countries had different health profiles and that the separation between them became substantially larger over the study period.
